title: PCIe root-complex locality and clock-transient effects: A100/H100/L40S comparative bench
body:
Summary:
This note summarizes an exploratory benchmark focused on two often-overlooked hardware/runtime interactions: (1) PCIe root-complex and inter-socket locality effects on inference latency/variance and (2) short-term GPU clock/transient behavior (clock boosts/drops) observed under bursty token-generation workloads. We compare representative cloud SKUs with A100, H100 and L40S GPUs across different driver/CUDA combos to identify practical mitigations for the serving runtime scheduler and instance selection recommendations for Dedicated/Private customers.

High-level findings (short):
- NVLink-enabled instance topologies consistently reduce tail latency for multi-GPU single-request sharding compared to PCIe-only topologies; differences are most pronounced at p95–p99 under 1–4ms per-token target workloads.
- Some PCIe-root-complex placements (e.g., GPUs attached to different CPU root complexes on multi-socket hosts) showed 8–22% higher p99 compared to GPUs on the same root complex, even when nominal NVLink was present but underutilized by our workload.
- H100 instances exhibited brief clock-boost drops during token burst > 512 tokens/second, correlated with power cap transitions in the driver (observed across two driver versions). L40S maintained more stable clocks under similar load.
- CUDA/driver combinations matter: CUDA 12.4 + nvidia-driver 535.x gave more consistent NVLink peer-to-peer throughput in our tests, while older driver stacks showed occasional link retraining events (seen in dmesg/nv_peer_memory logs) that aligned with microburst tails.

Goals and hypotheses:
- Goal: Quantify how topology (NVLink vs PCIe topology / root-complex locality) and transient clock behavior impact token latencies and tail behavior for common inference shapes.
- Hypothesis 1: When the runtime splits KV cache or attention state across GPUs, NVLink-local topologies eliminate a class of PCIe/CPU hops and thus reduce tail amplification under small-batch, low-latency targets.
- Hypothesis 2: GPU power/clock autoscaling in some SKUs introduces short windows of lowered clocks during sustained bursty requests, degrading p95/p99 for latency-sensitive tails.

Testbed summary:
- Clouds: AWS c7gn-like (PCIe-only), GCP a2/d2 variants (NVLink depending on SKU), Azure ND/NC-series variants. We selected a subset representative of our Dedicated offerings:
  - AWS: p4d-like (A100 x8 with NVLink), p4d-legacy PCIe variants (A100 x4 with PCIe aggregations)
  - GCP: A100 80GB (NVLink), L4/L40S instances (PCIe)
  - Azure: ND96ams (H100) and NC T4-like (PCIe)
- GPUs: A100 40/80GB, H100 80GB, L40S 48GB (where available).
- Drivers/CUDA: primary stacks tested: CUDA 11.8 + driver 515.x, CUDA 12.1 + driver 525.x, CUDA 12.4 + driver 535.x.
- Models/workloads: 7B (quantized int8), 13B (int8), 70B (fp16), generation targets with per-request prompt lengths 64–1024, prefix KV-cache pinned for sharded tests. Token generation mode: streaming, token-by-token with 8–16ms target inter-token times for latency-sensitive runs and burst mode (500–2000 tokens/sec) for throughput stress.
- Runtime config: our serving runtime in commit 3f9a7c (linked PR) run with persistent CUDA contexts enabled for all tests, with and without persistence-mode gpu-manager toggles. Batching: continuous batching disabled for latency tests; batch-packing windows varied from 2ms–50ms in sensitivity runs.

Instrumentation collected:
- Per-request p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side) and token-level latency histograms.
- GPU metrics: utilization, sm_clock, mem_clock, power_draw, temperature (nvidia-smi telemetry), NVLink TX/RX counters, PCIe throughput counters (where available), nvml events.
- dmesg and driver logs for link retraining/GPU resets.
- Host metrics: CPU socket topology, kernel dmesg, lspci topology map, interrupts per CPU.

Representative results (selected highlights):
1) p99 amplification vs topology (H100 A100 L40S mix, 13B model, 256 token steady gen)
   Topology                | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms)
   ------------------------|---------|---------|--------
   NVLink-local (same RC)  | 12.2    | 18.9    | 26.7
   PCIe-mixed (diff RC)    | 13.0    | 22.3    | 33.5
   PCIe-single (no NVLink) | 13.8    | 24.1    | 36.2
  Notes: p99 delta NVLink-local -> PCIe-single = +9.5ms (~36%).

2) H100 clock-transient observation (burst mode, 70B model, 1 client)
   - Under a ramp from idle to 1500 tokens/s sustained for ~10s, we observed periodic drops in sm_clock from 1650 MHz down to 1150 MHz lasting 80–240ms. Each drop aligned with a 2–5ms increase in token generation latency for the in-flight requests, with p99 moving from 42ms to 58ms during events.
   - dmesg showed repeated power cap negotiation logs on two H100 instances with driver 525.x; upgrading to 535.x reduced frequency of these events by ~75% in our runs.

3) NVLink throughput and retraining events (CUDA stacks)
   - On driver 515.x we saw NVLink peer-to-peer throughput variability +/- 15% and 1–2 small link retraining notices per 30-minute run during memory-hungry 70B shards.
   - CUDA 12.4 + driver 535.x removed retraining notices in equivalent runs and smoothed NVLink TX/RX counters.

Microbenchnotes and telemetry anomalies:
- PCIe root complex locality: two instances where GPUs sat on different root complexes showed increased host CPU interrupt spread and higher latency in PCIe DMA completions (measured via perf events), suggesting cross-RC PCIe traffic incurs additional host-side scheduling or IO path overheads.
- PCIe Gen mismatch: a GCP L40S PCIe v4 -> host PCIe v3 link retrained under heavy mem traffic and produced ~150–300us stalls periodically.
- Driver firmware/noise: a100 firmware on one AWS SKU had a known erratum that increased thermal/power throttling aggressiveness; we observed this as elevated temperature followed by clock drops even when absolute power was below SKU TDP.

Interpretation and root-cause hypotheses:
- Tail amplification in PCIe topologies is a combination of: cross-root-complex CPU path traversals + host interrupt scheduling + occasional PCIe link retraining leading to microstall events. These effects are amplified when runtime shards KV cache across GPUs and relies on peer-to-peer transfers during critical token generation windows.
- Clock-transient drops on H100 appear tied to driver/firmware interactions with power management; driver stacks with newer power-management heuristics may be aggressively capping clocks during short sustained bursts, whereas L40S vendors tuned for streaming workloads keep clocks stable.
- NVLink reduces the dependency on host CPU paths and removes a layer where device-to-device DMA would otherwise cross host PCIe. This explains consistent reductions in p95/p99 for sharded multi-GPU inference on NVLink topologies.

Practical recommendations (runtime + infra):
1) Scheduler/placement: prefer NVLink-local placements for any request that will split KV or attention state across GPUs. Add topology-awareness to the runtime scheduler (rank GPUs by NVLink adjacency and prefer same-RC GPUs).
2) Placement fallbacks: detect PCIe root-complex separation and prefer single-GPU placement or model-slicing strategies that avoid cross-GPU synchronous DMA during tight latency windows.
3) Driver/runtime flags: document and enable a "latency mode" for Dedicated instances that:
   - enables persistence-mode contexts and pre-allocates buffers at model load,
   - pins CUDA clocks to stable ranges (when allowed by policy) or requests conservative power-management heuristics,
   - sets a small warmup/prefetch phase to populate KV caches before returning the first token.
4) Instance selection guidance: for customers with strict p99 SLAs, recommend NVLink-capable SKUs (p4d-like, GCP NVLink A100) or L40S variants with stable clock behaviors rather than generic PCIe-only saturation-optimized SKUs.
5) Driver stack: standardize on CUDA 12.4 + nvidia-driver 535.x for Dedicated images in the short term; flag older stacks for investigation if customers see microburst tails.

Action items / follow-ups:
- INF-2310: Create a topology-aware scheduler RFC (owner: Jordan) to add NVLink adjacency scoring and RC-awareness into the placement heuristic.
- INF-2343: Run large-scale A/B across all SKUs with production traffic traces to validate real-world tail impact (owner: Asha).
- File driver/firmware bug with vendor for the observed H100 power/clock transient (owner: Ravi) and attach dmesg traces/telemetry.
- Short-term: bake an image with CUDA12.4 + driver 535.x and run a 72-hour soak of the 70B workflow to ensure no regression in cost or stability.

Caveats and limitations:
- Our tests skew toward single-request low-latency generation shapes; high-throughput batched workloads show different tradeoffs (PCIe is less problematic when larger amortized transfers dominate).
- Cloud SKU availability and exact PCIe/NVLink topologies vary by region and time; test results are representative of the SKUs we could provision during Jan 2025.
- Some telemetry counters are vendor-specific and were unavailable on a few managed SKUs; we inferred link events from dmesg in those cases.

Appendix: quick runbook for reproducing the two most actionable experiments
1) NVLink vs PCIe p99 bench (13B, 256 tokens):
   - Provision an NVLink-capable multi-GPU host and a PCIe-only host with similar CPU/IO specs.
   - Use serving runtime commit 3f9a7c, CUDA 12.4 + driver 535.x, persistence-mode ON.
   - Warmup: 200 requests of prefetched KV pads, then run 10k steady single-request generation at target inter-token 8ms.
   - Collect per-token latency, NVLink counters, and dmesg.

2) H100 transient clock observation (70B burst):
   - Provision H100 instance (ND-like), driver 525.x and 535.x variants.
   - Use a burst generator that ramps to 1500 tokens/s for 15s then idle 60s, repeat for 1 hour.
   - Collect sm_clock, power, and driver dmesg; look for clock drops aligned to power negotiation logs.

If you want, I can:
- Convert this note into a short RFC for the scheduler change and draft a placement algorithm pseudocode, or
- Produce a condensed 1-page summary for GTM/solutions engineering with recommended SKUs and customer messaging.

Raw test artifacts and scripts live at: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-scripts/tree/nvlink-locality (see run_pci_topo.sh and parse_nvlink_logs.py)

Prepared by: Maya Chen (serving runtime perf)
Reviewed: Jordan Lee, Asha Patel, Ravi Menon
